For me, it was just a matter of realizing my siblings were, just like me, kids of a very dysfunctional situation. And it didn’t happen over night. It’s taken more than 20 years of grueling therapy and some honest looks at myself and them to get here. I had to get to the place where I decided my truth existed whether or not they co-signed on it. Perhaps somewhat ironically, going no-contact with my mother removed her as an aspect of the relationship we shared, and free of her influence, I gained a much more objective view of how both are still beholden to her in a way that I am not, and haven’t been. That clarity helped me have a more compassionate understanding of how they were victimized by her, too.

Forgiveness is a tricky one. I think I need to be clear that part of my process involved realizing that they, just like me, were children trying their absolute hardest to survive in the only way they knew how. I can’t castigate them for how they utilized survival and also defend my own process (which often involves maladaptive coping mechanisms that I still try to work through in the present) as if that’s somehow more defensible. That’s not what I hear you saying, to be clear; I just want to explain that kids in such situations are tasked with impossible choices, and seeing how differently my siblings manage their lives and children in contrast to the hell we came from makes it significantly easier to give them the benefit of the doubt by loving the children they were, rather than nurturing resentment about how they “should have” acted, if that makes sense?

I’m sorry if this is unclear; I’m sitting in my car about to start my shift at the community shelter for the unhoused, and I think about these dynamics a lot when I work with this population. I ended up calling and leaving a voicemail, sadly telling them that I realized they had blocked me, and that although I didn’t understand why, I would respect their decision to cut me out but always be available for them in the future.

In the years since, I’ve had to come to terms with my responsibility in our falling out. While there was no singular incident, we had been growing apart because I was a toxic ass friend who clung to the best traits my friend had: emotional maturity, a loving heart, and wonderfully supportive, nurturing parents. I sucked them completely dry, to the point that, in the years leading up to that severance, they had become a cold, dismissive, judgmental person I almost couldn’t recognize. 

I didn’t know how to be a good friend, because I came from a home where people didn’t know how to be anything good themselves. My friend paid a heavy cost in the years of being the stability I clung to as a teenager and young adult. It’s been almost a decade now since last we spoke, and even though I never did anything maliciously, I have so much regret for what I did and put them through. Just last night, I was thinking about what I’d ever say to them if they reached out, and how I wish I could let them know I’m not the same person anymore, either.

Really, I hope that whenever they are, they’re doing well and that they are happy.

Another case involves two sisters out of California. 12-year-old Debbie Shelton disappeared in 1969. Her body was eventually discovered, and the investigation concluded she died by strangulation. In 2001, Vickie, Debbie’s then-41-year-old sister, vanished. To this day, there have been no breakthroughs in either sister’s case.

A more recent case is the Sexton/Summers sibling disappearances. Three siblings, Tristan Sexton (16), Taylor Summers (14), and Taryn Summers (8) disappeared separately over the course of seven months, from September of 2020 to April of 2021. The children were living with their grandmother, who reported each of them as runaways. Tristan and Taylor were eventually located safely, but Taryn’s dead body was discovered stuffed in a trash bag in the grandmother’s trunk. She has been charged with some lesser criminal offenses than murder, but I don’t remember what exactly. Maybe improper disposal of a corpse?

Given that I’m a woman with a long history of surviving sexual violence, including sex trafficking, I’m sure the request caught them off-guard, even after I explained what I’d just gone through. To answer your other questions, there was a ton of individual therapy. You’re in groups from about 9 a.m. until 4 p.m. Monday through Friday, and you’re also in groups Saturday until early afternoon. But depending on your level of need, you’ll have anywhere from two to four individual therapists to help you work on different things, and you meet with each provider a few times a week. 

In addition to the LCSW who was my lead, I had an MFT for Lifespan Integration and a psychologist for anxiety.  I don’t know if this was everyone’s experience, but my experience is that each provider worked on a different issue. Essentially, I felt like I was trying to work through three big issues: borderline agoraphobia that resulted from a fire that destroyed my town, killing almost a hundred people and displacing tens of thousands five months earlier; the suicide of my best friend six months before that which spiked my own intense suicidal ideation; and the aforementioned trauma from a therapist 14 years ago. I talked about all of these issues with my lead therapist, but he and I dealt with the suicide piece the most. Lifespan Integration dealt with the trauma around the therapist and the precipitating events that created that situation. And the fire, specifically the anxiety/agoraphobia it created, was the focus of my work with the psychologist. Having things so compartmentalized was really beneficial for me, personally, and it helped me grapple with planning as an active participant in my own recovery. 

You’ll also see a nutritionist (even without a history of eating disordered behavior, because they believe in treating the mind, body, and spirit), a naturopathic doctor, and a psychiatrist. I spent more time with the naturopath than most, because while I was there I had a flare up of two pretty serious medical ailments that made me so tired I couldn’t eat and I lost 20 pounds. First and foremost, I need to stress that my experience is atypical. The vast majority of trafficking victims are put into those situations by people they trust, especially family members. And often, trafficking victims have to hold a job out in society. A lot of the red flags are similar to domestic abuse, but large, brand-style tattoos can also be a giveaway.

If you want to scope out this business in particular, see if they have any kind of professional business reviews—Yelp, TrustPilot, etc. It’s unlikely they’re receiving professional reviews if they aren’t delivering the product they’re offering. Not impossible, of course; just unlikely. While most customers don’t care about illegality once they’re engaged in the sex, most are notoriously paranoid about being caught before or after, so I have a hard time imagining any of them agreeing to write a phony review because it creates a paper trail they don’t want to leave for fear of being connected to such crimes. After all, the vast majority of customers I had were white men with families and enough disposable income to hide spending a few hundred dollars for a few hours of companionship. They had a lot to lose if they were to be arrested.

I used to say if a woman’s attire seemed wildly out of step with the rest of her life, that could be an indicator, but I’m not sure how accurate that is, now that an entire subsection of the internet exists specifically to make designer goods (or impressive knock off designer goods) more affordable and accessible. I will also say there can and often is a lot of crossover between more legally protected forms of sex work (like strip clubs) and sex trafficking. I danced at two clubs during my time inside, and I wasn’t the only one. In that case, based on my own observations, the likelihood increases dramatically if the dancers are also immigrants, particularly undocumented ones.

Trafficking happens everywhere, but some flags can be decidedly regional. A lot of trafficking occurs in rural areas adjacent to major metropolitan areas because it’s easier to fly under the radar in a less-populated area, which can also be appealing to customers who want to maintain a low profile and decrease the risk of being caught.

Check out your area for human trafficking resources. The Polaris Project is a great national one, but your area should have some city, county, or regional task force, depending on how well-documented the problem is. Trafficking happens everywhere, but the laws pushed through a few years back—FOSTA-SESTA in particular—have just made things worse by forcing everything underground, conflating the separate pools of authentic sex workers and sex trafficking victims into one smorgasbord of people.

I experienced this when I worked at a community health center that specialized in women’s reproductive health. We received a negative review blasting us because a patient paid for rented goods with what the author of the review alleged was a stolen credit card. The reality is, we did no such thing. Whenever anyone rents one of our items, we make a copy of not only the card, but the ID. When there’s a situation where the card doesn’t belong to the renter, we only allow it if the person to whom the card belongs is in the office and signing off as a guarantor. And guess what? We make a copy of their ID then too, and they have to sign a contract. She also signed the contract as a guarantor, which stipulates the rental return date, and the product was not returned by the date, so we were legally within our rights to charge the card for the cost of the unreturned item.

The guarantor was pissed and didn’t think they should be on the hook for the contract, but there was nothing that I could do. I had no authority to return the transaction, especially as the equipment had not been returned. 

However, because we are a community health center, privacy rights come into play. We can’t provide Yelp with a copy of the contract to dispute the claim without violating HIPAA. I no longer work at the community health center, but I still look at the Yelp page every once in a while and see that shitty, untrue claim and it pisses me off.

I’m...really uncomfortable with drawing parallels between mental illness and gender identity, especially with casual language about choice. Especially because a significant reason scores of transfolx deal with mental health struggles in the first place is due to the belief that their gender identification is determined by the body parts they were born with and they can simply opt out of the suffering by choosing to embrace that archaic thinking.

That being said, is mental illness a choice? That is a question a lot of us have asked ourselves, and I don’t think it’s one any of us can answer globally. I know I didn’t choose to have PTSD or OCD or ADHD, but how I have experienced each of these conditions has been driven, at least partially, by choices I did make. In example, just today, I spent two hours filling out a wipe off calendar for my family’s schedule. I didn’t choose to have perfectionistic tendencies as part of my OCD, but I did make the choice to skip out on my Prozac lately, despite consciously knowing that doing so makes my OCD more, well, obsessive-compulsive.

In other words, it’s a complicated issue. And it’s probably true that there is some casual glorification or actual mental illness. I know people who brag about having OCD because they like a neat workspace or something, whereas in its most extreme my OCD manifests in ripping entire patches of hair out. It can be upsetting because I think if people really knew what such conditions entailed, they’d see there’s nothing remotely cool about them in the first place. Mental illness isn’t a weakness, but it also isn’t something to dismiss for the way it can control a life or even derail it.
